newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian car market sputters back to life.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian car market sputters back to life.

text.p: After four years of lethargy, the Italian car market is showing signs of getting into gear for a recovery, analysts and sector bodies said on Friday.

Better than expected new car registrations in December, coupled with prospects for new sales from a government car incentive scheme, mean now there is a "glimmer of hope" for the domestic auto market, the Italian car importers body Unrae said.

Leading sector research group CSP welcomed data published on Friday which showed new car registrations jumped 12.14 percent in December year-on-year and posted a modest 0.34 percent increase for 1996 as a whole.
Transport Ministry data showed new car registrations in 1996 rose to 1.74 million units and for December alone stood at 111,000 against forecasts for a rise of 102,000-105,000.

"This is a good figure. For December we were looking for somewhat less than the 12 percent rise. With the incentive scheme coming in this augurs well for 1997 figures," said car industry analyst Bob Barber at HSBC James Capel in London.
Italy's car market had a boom year in 1992 with total sales of 2.38 million. But the European car industry slumped in 1993.
Yet while Europe's top three car markets - Germany, France and Britain - have all since recovered, the continent's fourth largest market, Italy, has failed to pick up.
Unrae said the December figures showed the market clearly benefited from strong advertising campaigns by manufacturers.
But it said demand should be reinforced this year by the government's new scheme to boost car sales by giving motorists cash bonuses to scrap cars over 10 years old and buy new models.
"We should see a resulting acceleration in car demand but for this to be maintained we will still need to see a revitalisation of household consumption," Unrae said.
Barber noted that the French experience with incentives had seen positive effects on stimulating new car sales.

"It's a bit complicated here because the Italian scheme only runs for nine months to end-September. We saw in France a scramble to buy before the scheme ended, then a tailing off as it ended. An interesting question is whether after September there will be a vacuum or whether Italy will extend the incentives like France, and Spain, did," he said.
He said that as Italy has a very old car park, with some 30 percent of cars on the road over 10 years old, the incentives scheme could generate 100,000 to 150,000 extra sales.

CSP noted that already in December, before the government announced the scheme, car dealers were saying order books had begun to show an improvement with sales over the last 1996 quarter rising by 5.8 percent.
Its January survey, made after details of the government scheme were released, showed the amount of dealers expecting increased sales had risen from 16 percent in November to 55 percent.
CSP said the incentives are expected to result in extra sales of some 200,000 new cars. It forecast total 1997 sales at around 2.0 million against 1996's 1.74 million.
For 1997, including the effects of the scheme, Italian car manufacturers association Anfia forecast demand at between 1.95 and 2.0 million vehicles.
